text: Pigeons can tell people apart by their faces, even when those people change clothes.
People have trusted pigeons to carry messages for thousands of years, including during both World Wars.
A homing pigeon can find their way home from hundreds of miles away, using the sun and Earth's magnetic field.
A fluffed-up pigeon is wearing a built-in down jacket: the puffed feathers trap a layer of warm air.
House sparrows were brought to Brooklyn in 1852. Today they live on every continent except Antarctica.
Male sparrows with bigger black bibs tend to be the bosses of the flock.
Sparrow parents can raise three or even four families in a single summer.
Sparrows sleep together in thick bushes, packed in close for warmth and safety.
One squirrel can bury thousands of nuts in a single fall, each in its own spot.
A squirrel's front teeth never stop growing, so all that gnawing keeps them trim.
Gray squirrels don't hibernate. On the coldest days they just stay in the drey and nap.
A squirrel's tail is an umbrella, a blanket, a balance pole and a signal flag, all in one.
Every starling in North America comes from about 100 birds released in Central Park in 1890 and 1891.
In a swirling murmuration, each starling keeps track of just their seven closest neighbors.
Starlings' white winter spots wear off by spring, revealing glossy purple and green feathers.
Starlings can copy car alarms, phone ringtones and other birds' songs.
Doves can sip water like it's through a straw, without tipping their heads back like most birds.
Both mourning dove parents make a milky food in their throats to feed their chicks.
In warm places, a pair of mourning doves can raise up to six families in one year.
When a mourning dove takes off, their wings make a whistling sound, which might warn other doves.
Robins are often the first birds singing in the morning, sometimes before it's light out.
Robin eggs get their famous sky-blue color from a pigment called biliverdin.
Plenty of robins never fly south. They switch from worms to berries and travel in flocks.
Robins find worms by sight: that head tilt is them looking at the ground with one eye.
A herring gull takes about four years to grow their grown-up gray and white feathers.
Gulls can drink salt water. Special glands above their eyes get rid of the extra salt.
Gulls often spend the night floating on the water, safe from anything on land.
Gull chicks tap the red spot on a parent's beak to ask for food.
A raccoon's front paws have so many touch nerves that they can almost 'see' with their fingers in the dark.
Raccoons are puzzle experts who can remember how to solve a problem for years.
Raccoon babies are called kits, and they stay with their mom for nearly a year.
Raccoons don't hibernate, but in a cold snap they can sleep for days.
The monarchs flying south in fall can live eight or nine months. Summer monarchs live about a month.
Monarchs from all over the East fly to the same mountain forests in central Mexico.
A monarch caterpillar grows about 2,000 times bigger in just two weeks.
Monarchs taste with their feet, which is how they check a leaf is milkweed.
A red-tailed hawk can spot a mouse from 100 feet up.
Red-tailed hawk pairs often stay together for years and court again every winter.
Hawks ride rising columns of warm air, called thermals, to soar without flapping.
Young red-tails don't get their famous rusty-red tail until their second year.
A single blue jay can bury thousands of acorns in one fall.
Blue jays aren't really blue: tiny structures in their feathers scatter light so they look blue.
Blue jays are excellent hawk impersonators.
Near their nest, blue jays go quiet and sneaky, which is very unlike them.
Juncos often come back to the same winter neighborhood year after year.
Juncos are nicknamed snowbirds because they tend to show up just as it gets cold.
When a junco flies, white feathers flash on both sides of their tail.
In spring, juncos head north to raise their families in Canada and the mountains.
Opossums are North America's only marsupial: they carry their babies in a pouch.
An opossum has 50 teeth, more than any other North American land mammal.
Playing dead isn't a choice for opossums. It's an automatic response when they're very frightened.
A newborn opossum is about the size of a honeybee.
Crows can recognize individual human faces and remember them for years.
In fall and winter, crows gather at night in roosts that can hold thousands of birds.
Young crows often stay with their family for a few years and help raise their younger siblings.
Crows are clever problem-solvers who can figure out and use simple tools.
White-throated Sparrows come in two looks, white-striped and tan-striped, and usually pair up with the opposite one.
Their whistled song is often remembered as 'Oh sweet Canada, Canada, Canada.'
They spend the winter in thickets and leafy corners of city parks.
Males start singing in spring, before they fly north to their forests.
Chimney swifts can't perch on branches. Their tiny feet are made for clinging to walls.
Swifts glue their nests to chimney walls with their own sticky saliva.
At dusk, hundreds of swifts can funnel into one chimney to spend the night.
Chimney swifts spend the winter far away in the Amazon basin of South America.
Moths steer by keeping light above them, which is why a streetlight sends them in circles.
There are far more kinds of moths than butterflies: thousands in the Northeast alone.
While bees sleep, moths pollinate night-blooming flowers.
Many moths spend the winter as caterpillars or cocoons tucked in fallen leaves.
Canada Geese usually mate for life and raise their goslings as a team.
Goslings can walk, swim and feed themselves within a day of hatching.
Every summer, geese lose all their flight feathers at once and can't fly for about six weeks.
In a V, each goose rides the lift from the bird ahead, and they take turns leading.
The loud QUACK you know is almost always a female mallard. Males make a soft, raspy sound.
Mallards are the wild ancestors of almost every farm duck.
Mallard ducklings can swim and find their own food within hours of hatching.
In summer, male mallards trade their green heads for brown 'eclipse' feathers for a few weeks.
Brant fly thousands of miles from the Arctic tundra to spend the winter in New York Harbor.
Brant love sea lettuce, a bright green seaweed that grows on rocks along the shore.
Brant can drink salt water thanks to special glands that filter out the salt.
In spring, brant fatten up before a nonstop flight of thousands of miles back to the Arctic.
Cormorant feathers aren't fully waterproof, which helps them sink and dive after fish.
Cormorants swim underwater using their big webbed feet.
The 'double crest' is two little tufts of feathers that only show in breeding season.
Cormorants nest together in noisy colonies on the islands of New York Harbor.
The black ring near the tip of their beak is how you tell a ring-billed gull from a herring gull.
Ring-billed gulls often return to the same wintering spots year after year.
Young ring-billed gulls are mottled brown and take about three years to get their gray adult feathers.
At night, ring-billed gulls often sleep floating together on open water.
Common terns fly to South America and back every year.
A male tern courts with a gift: he offers the female a fresh fish.
Terns will swoop at people who get too close to their nests. Very brave for a small bird.
Terns hover in place over the water before diving headfirst for fish.
Great blue herons can stand still for a very long time, then strike at a fish in a split second.
Herons fly with their necks folded into an S; cranes fly with necks straight out.
Great blue herons nest together in tree colonies called rookeries.
A great blue heron can be over four feet tall but weighs only about five or six pounds.
Night herons' big red eyes help them see well enough to fish in the dark.
Young night herons are brown with white spots and look like a different bird entirely.
By day, night herons sleep in trees near the water, often in groups.
Black-crowned night herons live on every continent except Australia and Antarctica.
Buffleheads are one of the smallest ducks in North America.
Buffleheads nest in old woodpecker holes, and the ducklings jump down to the ground the day after they hatch.
A diving bufflehead can stay underwater for about 12 seconds, then pop up somewhere new.
Buffleheads arrive on our waters in late fall and stay until spring.
Mute swans aren't mute: they hiss, snort and grunt, and their wings whoosh loudly in flight.
Mute swans were brought from Europe in the 1800s to decorate parks and estates.
Cygnets sometimes ride on a parent's back, tucked between the wings.
A mute swan's nest can be a huge mound of reeds several feet across.
Male red-winged blackbirds can hide their red shoulder patches when they want to keep a low profile.
Red-winged blackbirds are one of the first birds to come back in spring.
Females are streaky brown and do most of the nest building, weaving nests into the reeds.
In fall, red-winged blackbirds gather in huge mixed flocks with grackles and starlings.
A deer's big ears can turn independently, like satellite dishes, to pick up sounds.
Fawns have very little scent, so mom leaves them hidden and still while she feeds nearby.
Bucks grow a new set of antlers every year and shed them in winter.
Deer are most active at dawn and dusk.
